name: Arak Bali
description: Balinese spirit distilled from palm sap or rice, made in village compounds across the island and used in Hindu offerings as well as in glasses. Legalised for licensed production in 2020 after decades in the grey market.
funFact: Arak is poured on the ground as part of Balinese Hindu offerings before ceremonies, which is one reason prohibition was never realistic.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, or as arak madu with honey and lime, which is the standard Balinese long drink. Buy licensed bottles; methanol adulteration in the informal trade has killed tourists and locals alike.

composition.summary: Palm sap or fermented rice distilled in village stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Coconut or palmyra palm sap, or fermented rice

composition.process: The 2020 governor's regulation created a licensed category specifically to displace unsafe production.

name: Cap Tikus
description: Sulawesi's palm spirit, distilled from tapped sugar-palm sap in the Minahasa highlands. The name means rat brand, which the makers have never bothered to explain or improve upon.
funFact: Minahasan tappers climb the sugar palms twice a day, and the sap is boiled down to palm sugar when it is not being distilled.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, which is how it is drunk in Minahasa. Some licensed producers now bottle a cleaner version; the village product is much stronger and considerably rougher.

composition.summary: Sugar-palm sap fermented and distilled repeatedly.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sap of the aren sugar palm

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Bamboo and pot stills, multiple runs for higher grades

composition.process: Grades are counted by how many times the spirit has been run through the still.

name: Ciu
description: Javanese cane moonshine, centred on Bekonang near Solo, where a whole village economy is built around small stills. Legal to produce as raw alcohol, ambiguous to sell as a drink, and widely drunk regardless.
funFact: Bekonang's distillers have operated for generations, officially producing industrial and medical alcohol while everyone understands where much of it ends up.

serve.how: Neat in small measures. Adulteration with methanol has caused repeated mass poisonings in Java, so this is a spirit where source is the only thing that matters.

composition.summary: Molasses or cane juice fermented and distilled in village stills.
composition.process: The same stills supply both drinking alcohol and legitimate industrial spirit, which blurs the regulation.

name: Sopi
description: The palm spirit of eastern Indonesia — Maluku, Flores, Timor — distilled from lontar or aren sap. The name comes from the Dutch zoopje, a small drink, and the tradition is centuries old.
funFact: In parts of Flores and Timor, sopi is required for customary ceremonies including marriage negotiations and dispute settlements.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, often from a bamboo cup, and always in company. It carries genuine ceremonial weight in eastern Indonesia and is offered before it is asked for.

composition.summary: Lontar or aren palm sap fermented and distilled over fire.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Bamboo or pot stills over wood fire

composition.process: Wood-firing the still is what gives eastern sopi its distinct smoke.

name: Lambanog
description: Filipino coconut spirit distilled from tuba, the fermented sap of the coconut flower, and traditionally bottled at around 80 proof. Quezon province makes most of it, and every fiesta there runs on it.
funFact: A single tapper may work dozens of palms a day, moving between crowns on bamboo poles rather than descending each tree.

serve.how: Neat in a shot glass, passed around a single glass in the traditional tagayan style where everyone drinks from the same one in turn. Flavoured versions with mango or bubblegum are popular and considerably sweeter.

composition.summary: Coconut flower sap fermented into tuba and distilled.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still, traditionally single, now often double

composition.process: Sap ferments within hours of tapping, so distilling has to follow the same day.

name: Ginebra San Miguel
description: The best-selling gin on the planet by volume, and almost all of it is drunk in the Philippines. Made since 1834, sweeter and lighter on juniper than a London Dry, and sold in the flat bottle known as a bilog.
funFact: It sells more cases a year than any other gin brand in the world, and has done for decades, largely on domestic consumption alone.

serve.glass: Shot glass, or highball for a gin pomelo
serve.how: Traditionally drunk in a tagayan circle from one shared glass, often with powdered juice mixed in — gin bulag. More conventionally, over ice with pomelo or calamansi soda.

composition.summary: Cane neutral spirit redistilled with juniper and botanicals.

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper and a light botanical blend

composition.process: A cane base rather than grain is what gives it a rounder, slightly sweeter body than European gin.

name: Philippine Rum
description: Rum distilled from Philippine molasses and aged in the tropics, of which Tanduay is the giant: a distillery running since 1854 that regularly out-sells nearly every rum brand in the world.
funFact: Tanduay has repeatedly ranked as one of the largest rum producers globally by volume, which surprises most people outside Southeast Asia.

serve.how: Over ice with cola or calamansi soda. The aged expressions take a single cube neat and carry more oak than the price suggests, given how fast tropical maturation moves.

composition.summary: Sugarcane molasses fermented, column-distilled and tropically aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Philippine sugarcane molasses, largely from Negros

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon oak in tropical conditions, five to sixteen years

composition.process: Negros island supplies most of the country's cane and is known domestically as the sugar bowl.

name: Lao Khao
description: Thailand's white spirit, distilled from sticky rice or molasses and sold in every provincial shop in the country. Cheap, strong and the base for the herbal infusions found in roadside ya dong stalls.
funFact: The name simply means white spirit, and it has been a state-licensed product since Thailand brought distilling under government monopoly in the nineteenth century.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, or with soda and lime. Most of it ends up steeped with roots and herbs as ya dong, sold by the shot from glass jars at roadside stalls.

composition.summary: Sticky rice or molasses fermented with a starter and distilled.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Look pang, a Thai yeast and mould starter

composition.process: Look pang works like Chinese qu, converting starch and fermenting in a single step.

name: Mekhong
description: Thailand's first domestically produced branded spirit, launched in 1941 from rice and molasses with a blend of herbs and spice. Marketed as Thai whisky for decades, it is closer to a spiced rum than to anything else.
funFact: It is the base of the Thai Sabai Sabai, essentially a Mai Tai variant, and was for years the only spirit most Thais could legally buy domestically.

serve.how: Over ice with soda and lime, or in a Sabai Sabai with lime and sugar. The spice blend gives it more character than its low strength suggests, and it works well in tiki-style builds.

composition.summary: Rice and molasses spirit blended with herbs and spices.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: A blend of Thai herbs and spices

composition.process: The spice blend is added after distillation, which is what separates it from a plain rum.

name: Ya Dong
description: Lao khao steeped with roots, bark and herbs in big glass jars, sold by the shot from roadside carts across Thailand. Every stall has its own recipes and every recipe claims a specific medicinal purpose.
funFact: Ya dong stalls typically serve each shot with a chaser of pickled fruit or a slice of guava with chilli salt, which is not optional.

serve.how: One shot, straight, with the pickled fruit chaser the vendor hands you. Different jars are sold for different complaints — aches, circulation, energy — and the vendor will steer you toward one.

composition.summary: Rice spirit macerated with medicinal roots, barks and herbs.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Dozens of roots, barks and herbs; recipes vary by stall

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for weeks in glass jars

composition.process: The jars keep infusing on the cart, so the same recipe changes over the course of a month.

name: Thai Rum
description: Agricole-style rum from fresh Thai cane juice, made by a small group of producers since 2012. Chalong Bay on Phuket distils from cane cut within hours and produces something notably grassy and clean.
funFact: Thailand's alcohol licensing made small-scale distilling nearly impossible until reforms in the 2010s opened the door to craft producers.

serve.how: In a daiquiri or with soda and lime, where the cane-juice grassiness shows best. The infused versions with lemongrass, kaffir lime or ginger work well in long drinks.

composition.summary: Fresh Thai sugarcane juice fermented and distilled.
composition.process: Cane is crushed within hours of cutting, since the juice degrades fast in tropical heat.

name: Rượu Đế
description: Vietnamese sticky-rice spirit, distilled in villages throughout the Mekong delta and the north. The name refers to the tall grass distillers once hid their stills in during the French colonial monopoly.
funFact: The French colonial administration monopolised alcohol production, which drove Vietnamese distillers into the fields and gave the spirit its name.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups, poured for others and drunk together on a toast. It appears at weddings, funerals and Tết, and refusing the first cup is difficult to do politely.

composition.summary: Glutinous rice fermented with a yeast starter and pot-distilled.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Men, a Vietnamese yeast and herb starter cake

composition.process: The men starter often contains herbs and spices as well as the culture, which carries into the spirit.

name: Rượu Thuốc
description: Vietnamese medicinal liquor: rice spirit steeped with ginseng, herbs, and frequently a snake, gecko or seahorse. Taken as a tonic, offered to guests, and photographed by every visitor who sees the jars.
funFact: Snake wine is made by submerging a live cobra in spirit, and the alcohol denatures the venom, which is protein-based and therefore neutralised.

serve.how: A small measure, taken for its supposed properties rather than its flavour. Vietnamese hosts offer it to guests as a mark of respect, and it is drunk in one rather than sipped.

composition.summary: Rice spirit steeped with herbs, roots or animal ingredients.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Ginseng, cordyceps, snake, gecko, seahorse, bark and roots

composition.process: High-proof spirit is used because it extracts and preserves in a way lower strengths cannot.

name: Vietnamese Gin
description: Gin built on foraged botanicals from Vietnam's northern highlands — mac mat leaf, Sichuan-style pepper, wild ginger, pomelo. Sông Cái opened the category in 2018 and buys from highland communities directly.
funFact: Sông Cái sources dozens of botanicals through highland farming communities in the northern mountains, several of which have no common English name.

serve.how: With a neutral tonic and a strip of pomelo peel, or in a Negroni where the wild-ginger note holds its own against Campari. Avoid heavily flavoured tonics; the foraged botanicals are subtle.

composition.summary: Rice or cane spirit redistilled with foraged highland botanicals.

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper plus mac mat, wild ginger, pomelo, cardamom, forest herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, some botanicals vapour-infused

composition.process: Botanicals are wild-harvested seasonally, so batches shift with what the mountains give.

name: Sraa Sar
description: Cambodian white rice spirit, distilled behind houses across the country in stills made from clay pots and salvaged metal. The everyday drink of rural Cambodia and the base of the infused versions sold to visitors.
funFact: Home distilling is widespread and largely unregulated in Cambodia, and most villages have at least one household producing for the neighbourhood.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, shared. It is rough on its own, which is why so much of it ends up infused with fruit and spice before it reaches anyone's glass.

composition.summary: Rice fermented with a starter and distilled in simple stills.
composition.process: Single distillation is the norm, which is why the base spirit is usually infused rather than drunk plain.

name: Sombai
description: Cambodian rice spirit infused with fruit and spice in decorated jars, made in Siem Reap. A modern product built on the traditional practice of steeping sraa sar, and the version most visitors actually enjoy.
funFact: The jars are hand-painted by local artists, and the decoration has become as much of the product as the liqueur inside.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or over ice with soda. Banana-cinnamon, ginger-red chilli and anise-coffee are the signature infusions, and they lean sweet, so keep the measure short.

composition.summary: Rice spirit macerated with fruit, spice and palm sugar.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Banana, ginger, anise, coffee, chilli, mango, palm sugar

composition.process: Palm sugar rather than cane sugar is used for sweetening, which keeps it distinctly Cambodian.

name: Lao-Lao
description: Laos's sticky rice spirit, distilled in villages along the Mekong and sold in whatever bottle is available, sometimes with a snake or scorpion inside. Cheap, strong and completely central to Lao social life.
funFact: At a Lao baci ceremony the same small glass is passed around the whole gathering, refilled each time, and everyone drinks from it in turn.

serve.how: Poured into one glass that passes around the circle, each person drinking and returning it. Refusing is awkward; taking a small sip and passing it on is not. Village strength varies enormously.

composition.summary: Glutinous rice fermented with a starter and pot-distilled.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: A local yeast and mould starter

composition.process: The snake and scorpion bottles are a separate infused product rather than the everyday spirit.

name: Htan Yay A-Yet
description: Burmese toddy palm spirit from the dry zone around Bagan, distilled from the fermented sap of the toddy palm. Sold at roadside stands with palm sugar sweets, and made in the same villages for generations.
funFact: Toddy palm climbers in the dry zone ascend with a bamboo ladder lashed to the trunk, and the profession is passed down within families.

serve.how: Neat in a small cup, usually alongside the palm sugar jaggery made from the same sap. Roadside toddy stands serve both, and the sweet cuts the spirit's rough edges.

composition.summary: Toddy palm sap fermented and distilled over wood fire.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sap of the toddy palm, tapped daily

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Clay or metal pot stills over wood fire

composition.process: The same sap is either drunk fresh, fermented into toddy, boiled to jaggery, or distilled.

name: Myanmar Rum
description: Rum distilled from molasses of cane grown along the Irrawaddy, made commercially since the colonial period. Dark, sweet and rarely seen outside the country or its immediate neighbours.
funFact: Myanmar's distilling industry dates to British Burma, and several brands still in production trace their origins to that period.

serve.how: Over ice with soda or cola, which is how it is drunk locally. It is sweet and simple, and the aged expressions take a cube neat well enough given how fast tropical maturation works.

composition.summary: Molasses from Irrawaddy cane fermented, distilled and aged.
composition.process: Central Myanmar's dry zone grows the cane, and the heat pushes maturation fast.

name: Samsu
description: A Malaysian and Singaporean cheap spirit distilled from cane or rice, often sold as a herbal or medicinal preparation to sidestep alcohol duty. Legal, unglamorous and drunk mostly by plantation workers.
funFact: Selling it as medicated samsu attracted a lower duty rate for years, which is why so many bottles carry herbal branding.

serve.how: Neat in small measures. Licensed samsu is safe; illicit versions have caused methanol poisoning outbreaks in Malaysia, so the distinction is worth paying attention to.

composition.summary: Cane or rice spirit, often infused with herbs.
composition.process: The herbal designation is a tax classification at least as much as a recipe.

name: Singapore Gin
description: A young category built on Southeast Asian botanicals — pandan, torch ginger, chrysanthemum, calamansi. Singapore had no distillery at all until Brass Lion opened in 2018, which for the home of the Singapore Sling was overdue.
funFact: Singapore had been without a working distillery for decades before Brass Lion, despite lending its name to one of the world's most famous cocktails.

serve.how: With a light tonic and a wedge of calamansi, or in a Singapore Sling made properly with cherry brandy and Bénédictine. The pandan note is delicate, so avoid a heavy tonic.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit redistilled with Southeast Asian botanicals.

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, pandan, torch ginger, chrysanthemum, calamansi, lemongrass

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still with vapour infusion

composition.process: Vapour infusion is used for the most delicate botanicals, which would be cooked out by maceration.

name: Tua Sabu
description: Timor-Leste's palm spirit, distilled from the sap of lontar and coconut palms in villages across the country. Made informally, drunk at every ceremony, and central to Timorese social life.
funFact: Tua sabu is required at Timorese customary ceremonies, and efforts to formalise its production have focused on safety rather than restriction.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, shared. Quality varies widely between makers, and there have been poisoning incidents from adulterated batches, so a known source matters.

composition.summary: Lontar or coconut palm sap fermented and distilled over fire.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Bamboo and pot stills over wood fire

composition.process: Bamboo is used for both the still's condenser and the serving vessel in traditional production.

name: Australian Whisky
description: Tasmania leads a category barely thirty years old, using small casks, maritime air and a climate that matures spirit fast. Australian single malts have taken world titles against far older distilling nations.
funFact: Distilling was illegal in Tasmania from 1839 until Bill Lark had the law overturned in 1992, which is why the whole industry is so young.

serve.how: Neat with a drop of water. Small casks mean heavy wood extraction, so water pulls the spirit forward. Many are bottled at cask strength and non-chill-filtered, where dilution genuinely helps.

composition.summary: Malted barley distilled and matured in small casks in Tasmania.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: 100 and 200 litre ex-fortified-wine casks, two years and up

composition.process: Ex-apera and ex-tokay casks from Australian fortified wine producers are the local signature.

name: Australian Rum
description: Queensland molasses rum, of which Bundaberg is the national icon and Beenleigh the oldest, running since 1884. Sweet, heavy and inseparable from Australian drinking culture, particularly north of Brisbane.
funFact: The 1808 Rum Rebellion, the only successful armed takeover of government in Australian history, was triggered partly by attempts to control the rum trade.

serve.how: With cola and ice, which is how the overwhelming majority is drunk. The aged and small-batch releases from Beenleigh and Bundaberg's Master Distillers series deserve a rocks glass and a single cube.

composition.summary: Queensland molasses fermented and distilled, then oak-aged.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon and ex-fortified oak, two years and up

composition.process: Beenleigh has run since 1884, making it one of the oldest continuously operating distilleries in the southern hemisphere.

name: Australian Gin
description: Gin built on native botanicals that grow nowhere else — lemon myrtle, wattleseed, pepperberry, finger lime, strawberry gum. Australia went from almost no gin distilleries to hundreds in a decade.
funFact: Four Pillars' Bloody Shiraz gin is made by steeping whole shiraz grapes in gin for eight weeks, which turns it deep purple.

serve.glass: Large copa with plenty of ice
serve.how: With a dry tonic and a wedge of grapefruit or a few native pepperberries. Lemon myrtle is intensely citrusy on its own, so adding lime tends to be redundant rather than complementary.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit redistilled with juniper and Australian native botanicals.

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper plus lemon myrtle, wattleseed, pepperberry, finger lime, river mint

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, often with vapour baskets

composition.process: Many native botanicals are harvested by Indigenous-owned enterprises, which several distilleries source from directly.

name: Bush Tucker Liqueur
description: Liqueurs made from Australian native fruits — Davidson plum, quandong, riberry, muntrie — most of which have no equivalent anywhere else and only entered commercial cultivation in the last few decades.
funFact: Davidson plum is intensely sour and almost inedible raw, which is exactly why it works so well steeped and sweetened.

serve.glass: Small cordial glass or over ice
serve.how: Cold and neat after dinner, or topped with sparkling wine. The tartness of Davidson plum and quandong makes them better in a spritz than most fruit liqueurs, which tend to cloy.

composition.summary: Native Australian fruit macerated in neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Davidson plum, quandong, riberry, muntrie, finger lime

composition.process: Most of these fruits are still wild-harvested or grown at very small scale, which keeps production tiny.

name: New Zealand Whisky
description: A category that died and came back: New Zealand's last big distillery closed in 1997, its stock was bought by a collector, and new distilleries have since started from scratch in Otago and beyond.
funFact: When the Willowbank distillery in Dunedin closed, its remaining casks were bought en masse and bottled over the following two decades as the country's only aged stock.

serve.how: Neat with a drop of water. The rescued Willowbank stock is now genuinely old and worth treating carefully; the new-make from the modern distilleries is younger and takes water more readily.

composition.summary: Malted barley distilled and matured in New Zealand.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Ex-bourbon and ex-wine casks; the old Willowbank stock ran past 20 years

composition.process: A cool maritime climate means slow maturation, closer to Scotland than to Tasmania.

name: Hokonui Moonshine
description: Southland's illicit whisky, distilled in the Hokonui hills by Scottish settlers through a local prohibition that ran from 1902 to 1954. Now legal, and made openly by the descendants of people who did not.
funFact: Invercargill and the surrounding district voted itself dry in 1902, and the Hokonui hills supplied the region illegally for over fifty years.

serve.how: Neat or with a splash of water. The peated versions carry real smoke, drawn from Southland peat rather than Islay. It is a young whisky and drinks like one, which is part of the appeal.

composition.summary: Malted barley, often peated with local peat, distilled in Southland.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Some unaged in the moonshine style, some oak-matured

composition.process: Southland peat gives a different smoke profile from Scottish peat, being younger and more vegetal.

name: New Zealand Gin
description: Gin built on native flora — horopito, kawakawa, mānuka, kelp, and the citrus that grows well in the north. A small but unusually inventive scene, helped by a country where almost everything botanical is endemic.
funFact: Horopito is known as the pepper tree and carries a genuine chilli-like heat, which comes through clearly in a gin distilled with it.

serve.how: With a dry tonic and a slice of feijoa or grapefruit. Horopito's peppery heat builds, so a lighter tonic and a citrus garnish keep it in balance rather than letting it dominate.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit redistilled with juniper and New Zealand natives.

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Juniper, horopito, kawakawa, mānuka, kelp, citrus peel

composition.process: Some producers use whey spirit from the dairy industry as their base, which is distinctly New Zealand.

name: Feijoa Liqueur
description: Made from a South American fruit that New Zealand adopted so completely that most New Zealanders assume it is native. Aromatic, tart and almost impossible to describe to anyone who has not eaten one.
funFact: Feijoas fall from the tree when ripe rather than being picked, which is why they barely travel and are almost unknown outside a few countries.

serve.glass: Small glass, or highball with soda
serve.how: Cold and neat, or with soda over ice, which suits the tartness better than tonic. It also works topped with sparkling wine. The vodka-based versions are cleaner than the cream ones.

composition.summary: Feijoa fruit macerated or distilled into neutral spirit and sweetened.
composition.process: The fruit oxidises within minutes of being cut, so it has to be processed almost immediately.

name: Fijian Rum
description: Column-still rum from Lautoka cane, made with unusually long fermentations that build a fruity, ester-rich spirit. Fiji's sugar industry is over a century old, and the rum is finally getting attention abroad.
funFact: Fermentation at the Lautoka distillery can run several times longer than industry standard, which is where the pronounced fruit character comes from.

serve.how: Neat for the aged expressions, or in a daiquiri where the ester-driven fruit does most of the work. It has enough character to stand in for Jamaican rum in a tiki build.

composition.summary: Fijian molasses fermented long and column-distilled.
composition.process: Extended fermentation builds esters, which is the same principle Jamaican distillers use to make funk.

name: Rhum de Tahiti
description: Agricole rum from French Polynesia, distilled from cane grown on Taha'a and Tahiti. A tiny production in the middle of the Pacific, made in the French island tradition and almost never seen elsewhere.
funFact: Cane was reintroduced commercially to Taha'a specifically to supply the distillery, having largely disappeared from the islands.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, or in a Ti' Punch with lime and cane syrup as the French islands drink it. The floral character is delicate and gets buried by anything heavier.

composition.summary: Fresh Polynesian cane juice fermented and column-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh-pressed cane from Taha'a and Tahiti

composition.process: The volcanic soil and heavy rainfall of the Society Islands give a notably floral cane.

name: Hawaiian Rum
description: Rum from the last of Hawaii's sugar cane, an industry that dominated the islands for a century and closed its final mill in 2016. Small distilleries now grow their own cane to keep making it.
funFact: Hawaii's last commercial sugar plantation closed in 2016, so distilleries there now cultivate their own cane specifically for rum.

serve.how: In a Mai Tai made properly with lime, orgeat and curaçao, or neat for the aged bottlings. The cane-juice versions are grassy and bright and make an excellent daiquiri.

composition.summary: Hawaiian cane juice or molasses fermented and distilled.
composition.process: Several distilleries grow heirloom Hawaiian cane varieties that the plantations had abandoned.

name: Steamit
description: Papua New Guinean home-distilled spirit, made from whatever will ferment — sugar, fruit, cassava — in improvised stills. Illegal, widespread, and known by the pidgin word for what comes off the still.
funFact: Papua New Guinea has periodically debated regulating steamit rather than prosecuting it, on the same public health logic Kenya applied to chang'aa.

serve.how: Neat, in small measures, and with real caution. It is entirely unregulated, frequently very strong, and adulteration is a genuine hazard rather than a theoretical one.

composition.summary: Sugar, fruit or cassava fermented and distilled in improvised stills.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sugar, fruit, cassava or sweet potato

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Improvised stills from drums and pipe

composition.process: Nothing about production is standardised, which is why strength and safety vary batch to batch.
